newsitem.title: GERMANY: Greens elect east German teacher as new co-leader.
newsitem.headline: Greens elect east German teacher as new co-leader.

text.p: Germany's opposition Greens elected 34-year old schoolteacher Gunda Roestel as their new co-leader on Saturday, hoping the former East German citizen would help boost their fortunes in the former communist region.
Roestel was elected unopposed at a congress in the eastern town of Suhl to the co-leadership post the fiercely egalitarian party reserves for a female candidate.
She replaced Krista Sager, who quit the post to concentrate on next year's local elections in her home city of Hamburg.

The Greens, who have grown to become Germany's third political force from their origins in the peace movement and student demonstrations of the 1960s and 1970s, re-elected Juergen Trittin to their other co-leadership post.
"I will work for the whole party just as the whole party must work to build up the east," Roestel told around 750 delegates at the conference.
The Greens are anxious to make more progress in eastern Germany, which accounts for a fifth of the national population but only seven percent of their party membership.
Delegates also passed resolutions on tax reform and other economic policies in a bid to portray themselves as a mature party capable of helping to topple Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
"We must ensure Kohl doesn't continue his political retirement in the chancellery," Roestel said. "It's our job to provide new political orientation."
The Greens hope to form a coalition with the main opposition Social Democrats (SPD) after the 1998 general election.
Roestel, the director of a school for handicapped children in the state of Saxony, grew up under communism in East Germany but never joined the ruling party.

She was active in local church groups and was removed from a teaching post in 1989 by communist authorities after applying to leave the country. The East German state collapsed later that year and Roestel subsequently won her job back.
Political analysts say the Greens are often weak in the east because they are seen as having no real answers to the region's higher unemployment and industrial decline.
Keen to prove they can act as more than just the nation's environmental conscience, the conference delegates approved a plan for a radical reform of the tax system.
The basic rate of income tax would fall by almost six points to 20 percent under the plan, designed to reduce taxes for low earners, hit the rich harder and curtail tax evasion.
Opinion polls show the Greens attracting around 12 percent support nationally -- more than double the rating for the traditional third party, the liberal Free Democrats (FDP).
Polls also show if the SPD and Greens maintained current levels of support they would be able to oust the centre-right coalition of Kohl's Christian Democrats and the FDP in 1998.
